title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
scopeHtml: Scope: LoRA, QLoRA, full fine-tuning, hyperparameters, evaluation and deployment.

notes.title: Full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient
notes.html:
Full fine-tuning (FFT). Update all weights with gradient descent on your data.

  • Memory: weights + gradients + optimizer states. With AdamW in mixed precision it's roughly 16 bytes per parameter (2 weights bf16 + 2 grads + 4 master weights fp32 + 8 for Adam moments): a 7B model needs ~110 GB, a 70B model >1 TB before sharding/activations. Techniques: ZeRO/FSDP sharding, gradient checkpointing, 8-bit optimizers.
  • Pros: highest capacity to adapt, best for large distribution shifts or continued pretraining.
  • Cons: costly, risk of catastrophic forgetting, one full model copy per task (storage and serving), harder to roll back.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). Freeze base weights; train a small number of extra parameters (0.01 to 2% of the model). Benefits: far less memory (no optimizer state for the frozen base), small artifacts (MBs), multiple tasks sharing one base, easy rollback, less forgetting. Cost: slightly lower ceiling on some hard tasks (often negligible).

Families. LoRA/QLoRA (low-rank adapters), (IA)³, prefix/prompt tuning, adapters (bottleneck layers), BitFit (bias only), DoRA and LoRA variants.

Choosing. Start with LoRA/QLoRA; move to full fine-tuning only if evals show a quality gap that more rank/targets can't close and you have the compute.

Real life. Repainting a whole house versus hanging a few new pictures and swapping them when needed.

notes.title: LoRA
notes.html:
Idea. For a weight matrix W (d × k), learn a low-rank update ΔW = B·A with A (r × k), B (d × r), r ≪ min(d, k). Forward: y = Wx + (α/r)·B(Ax). Only A and B are trained; A is initialized randomly, B to zero so training starts from the base model. Trainable parameters per matrix: r(d + k) instead of d·k.

Example. d = k = 4096, r = 16: 131k parameters vs 16.8M (0.8%). Applied to all attention (and MLP) projections of a 7B model: ~20 to 80 M trainable parameters.

Hyperparameters.

  • Rank r (8, 16, 64): capacity; higher for complex tasks; diminishing returns.
  • Alpha α: scaling (commonly α = r or 2r); effective step size.
  • Target modules: attention q,k,v,o and often MLP gate/up/down; more targets = more capacity.
  • Dropout (0 to 0.1) to regularize.
  • Learning rate: higher than full fine-tuning (1e-4 to 3e-4), cosine/linear decay with warmup.
  • Batch size/epochs: 1 to 3 epochs for most instruction datasets.

Serving.

  • Merge the adapter into the base weights (W' = W + BA) for zero inference overhead, but you lose swap-ability.
  • Dynamic adapters: keep the base loaded and apply adapters per request (multi-LoRA serving: S-LoRA, vLLM LoRA) — efficient multi-tenant customization.

Code sketch.

from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
cfg = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                 target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj","gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj"],
                 task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
model = get_peft_model(base_model, cfg)   # base frozen, adapters trainable

Real life. A removable overlay on a map instead of redrawing the map.

notes.title: QLoRA
notes.html:
Idea. Quantize the frozen base model to 4-bit (NormalFloat4, NF4) with double quantization, keep LoRA adapters in bf16, backprop through the dequantized weights, and use paged optimizers to handle memory spikes. Result: fine-tune a 65 to 70B model on a single 48 to 80 GB GPU, or a 7 to 13B model on a consumer GPU, with quality close to 16-bit LoRA.

Memory arithmetic. 70B in NF4 ≈ 35 to 40 GB for weights, plus activations/adapters/optimizer for the LoRA params (tiny), so ~48 GB total with gradient checkpointing vs >1 TB for full fine-tuning.

Trade-offs. Slower than bf16 LoRA (dequantization overhead, ~20 to 40%); small quality loss; the quantized base affects the final merged model, so merge into a 16-bit copy or re-quantize carefully and re-evaluate.

Real life. Working from a compressed copy of the textbook while writing your notes in full resolution.

notes.title: Training practices
notes.html:
Setup checklist.

  1. Choose the base model (instruct vs base, size, licence, tokenizer, context length).
  2. Format data with the exact chat template; mask loss on prompt tokens (train on assistant tokens).
  3. Pack or bucket sequences by length for efficiency; handle max length without truncating answers.
  4. Hyperparameters: LoRA lr ~2e-4 (full FT ~1e-5), warmup 3 to 10%, cosine decay, weight decay 0 to 0.1, batch size 16 to 128 effective, 1 to 3 epochs.
  5. Precision: bf16 mixed precision; gradient checkpointing for memory; FlashAttention.
  6. Monitor: training loss, validation loss every N steps, sample generations, grad norm, learning rate; log to W&B/MLflow.
  7. Early stopping/checkpoint selection by validation loss and task eval (loss isn't the metric you care about).

Diagnosing curves. Train loss falling, validation loss rising = overfitting (reduce epochs/rank, more data, regularize). Both flat = too low LR/too little capacity/bad data. Spikes = LR too high, bad batches. Training loss near zero quickly = memorization or leakage.

Catastrophic forgetting. Narrow fine-tuning degrades general abilities. Mitigate: LoRA/low rank, low LR, fewer epochs, mix general instruction data (5 to 30%) into the training set, replay data, regularization (e.g. KL to base), evaluate on general benchmarks and safety probes.

Reproducibility. Fix seeds, record data/config/code versions, store checkpoints and the evaluation reports.

Real life. Coaching an athlete: enough training to improve, not so much that they're injured or forget other skills.

notes.title: Evaluating and deploying
notes.html:
Evaluation.

  • Task metrics on the held-out test set vs baselines (prompted base, stronger model).
  • Behavioural checks: format validity rates, refusal behaviour, tool-calling accuracy, long-input handling.
  • Regression suite: general benchmarks and in-house probes.
  • Safety: red-team prompts; fine-tuning can erode safety behaviour, so re-test.
  • Human review of samples; LLM judge calibrated.
  • Cost/latency: tokens saved, throughput on target hardware.

Deployment options.

  • Hosted fine-tuning APIs (simple; limited model choice/control; data leaves your environment; check retention terms).
  • Self-hosted: vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM serving the merged model or multi-LoRA.
  • Quantize for serving (AWQ/GPTQ/FP8) and re-evaluate.

Operations. Version datasets, configs, adapters and evaluation reports together; canary rollout with the base model as fallback; monitor drift (new topics, formats); retraining triggers (new data volume, metric decay, requirement changes); retention and deletion of training data (privacy).

Real life. Road-testing a tuned car before it goes on sale, then watching warranty claims.

notes.title: Alternatives and related methods
notes.html:
• Prompt/prefix tuning: learn soft prompt vectors; very light but usually weaker than LoRA.
  • Adapters (bottleneck layers): add small modules; add inference latency unless fused.
  • Continued pretraining: further next-token training on domain text (legal, biomedical, code) to absorb vocabulary and style before SFT; expensive, needs lots of text.
  • Preference optimization (DPO, KTO, ORPO) to shape quality and safety after SFT.
  • Distillation: train a small student from a strong teacher's outputs (see optimization notes).
  • Model merging (weight averaging, TIES, DARE) to combine skills without training; experimental, evaluate carefully.
  • Embedding/reranker fine-tuning for retrieval with (query, positive, hard negative) triples.
  • Hosted vs open weights: hosted is convenient; open weights give control and portability.

Choosing. Start with the lightest approach that clears the eval: prompt → LoRA SFT → add preference tuning if needed → full fine-tune/continued pretraining only with strong evidence.

Real life. Choosing between a tailored suit, alterations, and off-the-peg.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
FFT vs PEFT. Full fine-tuning updates everything (~16 bytes/param with AdamW, risk of forgetting, one model per task). PEFT freezes the base and trains tiny modules; LoRA is the default.

LoRA. ΔW = BA with rank r; trainable ≈ r(d+k) per matrix; hyperparameters rank, alpha, target modules, dropout, LR ~1e-4 to 3e-4; merge for zero overhead or serve multi-LoRA adapters per tenant. QLoRA adds 4-bit NF4 base + paged optimizers, enabling 70B fine-tuning on one big GPU at slight speed/quality cost.

Training. Exact chat template, loss on assistant tokens only, 1 to 3 epochs, warmup + decay, monitor validation loss and real task metrics, early stop; mitigate forgetting with low rank/LR and general-data replay; fix seeds and version everything.

Evaluation and deployment. Compare to prompted baselines; check regressions, safety, format validity, cost/latency; hosted API vs self-hosted; quantize and re-test; canary with fallback; retraining triggers; privacy for training data.

Alternatives. Prompt tuning, adapters, continued pretraining, DPO/KTO/ORPO, distillation, model merging, retriever fine-tuning.

Interview one-liners.

  • "LoRA trains a low-rank delta; merge it for free inference or keep it swappable."
  • "QLoRA = 4-bit frozen base + bf16 adapters."
  • "Validation loss is not your metric; run the task eval."
  • "Fine-tuning can erode safety and general skills: test for regressions."
